q: A company is moving 40 on-premises databases whose stored procedures join across databases with three-part names and depend on SQL Agent jobs and Database Mail. They want minimal code changes, and nobody on the team wants to own OS or engine patching. Which target fits best?
opts: Azure SQL Managed Instance in the General Purpose tier
An Azure SQL Database elastic pool, using elastic query to replace the cross-database joins
SQL Server on an Azure VM, with Azure Update Manager scheduling the patches
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale with one database per application area
why: Managed Instance is instance-scoped PaaS: three-part-name queries, SQL Agent, and Database Mail work with little change, and Microsoft patches the OS and engine. An elastic pool of single databases has no SQL Agent or Database Mail, and elastic query is a rewrite, not a drop-in replacement for cross-database joins. A VM can have its patching scheduled through Azure Update Manager, but the team still owns the OS, the patch schedule, and the testing, which the scenario rules out. Hyperscale is a single-database tier and has the same instance-feature gaps.

q: A production database runs on the DTU-based Standard tier. The company owns SQL Server Enterprise licenses with Software Assurance and wants to use them to lower the compute bill without leaving the PaaS platform. What should the DBA do?
opts: Convert the database to the vCore purchasing model, then apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to it
Turn on Azure Hybrid Benefit for the DTU database, which converts license cores into DTUs
Move to SQL Server on an Azure VM, since license reuse is a benefit reserved for virtual machines
Place the database in an elastic pool, which lets licenses offset eDTU charges
why: Azure Hybrid Benefit applies to vCore-based compute, and a DTU database can be moved to a vCore service objective in place, so license reuse and PaaS are compatible. There is no mechanism that translates license cores into DTUs, so that option does not exist. PaaS vCore databases can use Hybrid Benefit, so abandoning PaaS for a VM is unnecessary. Pooling changes how compute is shared, not how it is licensed, and eDTU pools are still DTU-based.

q: A trading application on a stable 400 GB database needs the lowest possible storage latency and a readable replica for reporting that adds no extra replica compute charge. No cross-region requirement exists. Which configuration fits?
opts: General Purpose with zone-redundant configuration enabled
Hyperscale with a named replica sized for the reporting load
General Purpose serverless with a raised maximum vCore setting
Business Critical with read scale-out used by the reporting connections
why: Business Critical keeps data on local SSD and already runs secondary replicas for HA; read scale-out lets reporting use one of them at no additional replica charge. General Purpose uses remote storage (higher latency), and zone redundancy does not add a readable replica. A Hyperscale named replica is readable but is extra billed compute, and Hyperscale's remote page servers are tuned for size and scale rather than lowest local-SSD latency. Serverless General Purpose is still remote storage with no readable secondary.

q: A SaaS provider hosts 200 single-tenant databases that peak at different times of day. One large tenant occasionally runs a heavy batch job, and the provider wants cost minimized without letting that tenant starve the others. What should they implement?
opts: Serverless single databases with auto-pause enabled on each tenant
An elastic pool sized for aggregate demand, with a per-database maximum set below the pool maximum
One elastic pool left at default per-database settings so tenants can borrow the full pool
A Hyperscale database per tenant, each with its own named replica
why: Pooling shares one billed resource budget across databases with staggered peaks, and a per-database maximum caps how much of that budget any one tenant can consume, which contains the batch job. Serverless with auto-pause suits idle databases, not 200 active tenants whose compute is billed individually. Default per-database settings leave the noisy-neighbor problem unsolved, since one tenant can take the whole pool. Hyperscale per tenant sizes and bills each database separately and adds named-replica cost, defeating the savings goal.

q: A reporting database is busy for about three hours each weekday, with load ranging from light to heavy, and idle overnight and on weekends. The team wants compute billed by actual use with no scheduled scaling scripts, and can tolerate a delay on the first connection after an idle period. Which configuration fits?
opts: Provisioned General Purpose, scaled up and down each day by an Azure Automation runbook
General Purpose serverless with a minimum and maximum vCore range and auto-pause
Business Critical provisioned and sized for the heaviest expected load
A DTU Standard database placed in a pool with other continuously busy databases
why: Serverless scales compute inside a configured vCore range, bills per second of use, and auto-pauses when idle, billing storage only, so it needs no scheduling scripts and the stated cold-start tolerance is exactly its tradeoff. The runbook approach can work but is the scripted administration the team wants to avoid and still bills provisioned compute at every size. Business Critical sized for peak pays for the peak around the clock. Pooling with always-on databases ties the cost to their load and does not pause anything.

q: A DBA must move an on-premises SQL Server 2016 database to Azure SQL Database. Several stored procedures use features the DBA suspects are unsupported. Which action should be taken first?
opts: Run a migration assessment to find blocking compatibility issues and get a target SKU recommendation
Start an online Azure Database Migration Service run and fix errors as they appear
Back up to a .bak file in Blob Storage and restore it with RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM URL
Export a BACPAC and import it into a new database, then review failures in the import log
why: Assessment (formerly the Data Migration Assistant or the Azure SQL Migration extension, both now retired; today use the assessment experiences in Azure Arc, Azure Migrate, and SSMS) surfaces blocking and deprecated features and sizes the target before any data moves, so problems are found while they are cheap to fix. Starting a migration first discovers the same issues mid-flight. A native .bak restore is not supported by Azure SQL Database at all (it works for Managed Instance), so it fails regardless. A BACPAC import is offline and would only reveal incompatibilities after the downtime has started.

q: Azure SQL Managed Instance can restore a database from a native SQL Server .bak file stored in Azure Blob Storage, even though it is a PaaS service.
opts: True
False
why: Managed Instance supports native RESTORE ... FROM URL for .bak files, which is one of the main reasons it is the low-friction migration target for existing SQL Server databases. Azure SQL Database single databases do not support native backup restore, which is why people assume PaaS never does.

q: A DTU-based database can be changed to a vCore-based service objective in place, without exporting and re-importing the data.
opts: True
False
why: Changing the purchasing model is performed like a scale operation: the existing database moves to a vCore service objective while staying online apart from a brief reconnect at the end. No BACPAC round trip is needed, which also means Azure Hybrid Benefit is reachable for an existing DTU database.

q: After a serverless database auto-pauses, its first connection attempt always succeeds after a short delay, so the application needs no connection retry logic.
opts: True
False
why: Resuming from a pause takes time, and a login that arrives during the resume can fail with a database-unavailable error before a later attempt succeeds, so the delay is not guaranteed to be transparent. That is why serverless suits dev/test and intermittent workloads, and why apps on it need transient-fault retry handling.

q: Which two statements about Azure SQL Database service tiers are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A General Purpose database recovers from a node failure by attaching new compute to its remote storage
Business Critical includes a readable secondary replica that read scale-out can use at no extra replica charge
Business Critical keeps its database files on remote Azure Premium storage shared between the replicas
Hyperscale backups are taken by streaming the full database to Blob Storage nightly
Enabling zone redundancy on General Purpose adds a readable secondary for read scale-out
why: General Purpose separates compute from remote storage, so a failed node is replaced by new compute attached to the same storage, and Business Critical's built-in replicas are readable through read scale-out at no added replica charge. Business Critical uses local SSD on each replica, not shared remote storage. Hyperscale uses storage snapshots, not nightly full streams. Zone redundancy on General Purpose spreads storage and standby compute across zones but adds no readable secondary.

q: Heavy reporting queries slow OLTP traffic on a General Purpose database. The team will accept a tier change but wants read-only traffic served by a replica that already runs for high availability, selected only by a connection-string setting, with no extra replica cost. What should they do?
opts: Move to Business Critical and set ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly on the reporting connections
Move to Hyperscale and add a named replica with its own database name for reporting
Add an active geo-replication secondary in another region and point reports at it
Keep General Purpose and enable read scale-out on the database
why: Business Critical already runs HA replicas, and read scale-out routes connections that declare read-only intent to one of them at no added replica charge. A Hyperscale named replica is a separate, billed compute resource reached by its own database name, not by intent. A geo-replication secondary is another billed database with its own server name. General Purpose has no readable HA replica, so read scale-out cannot be enabled there.

q: A General Purpose single database can use read scale-out, because every Azure SQL Database tier keeps at least one readable secondary replica for high availability.
opts: True
False
why: General Purpose relies on remote storage and replaces a failed compute node rather than keeping a readable secondary, so read scale-out is not available there. It is offered on Premium and Business Critical (and Hyperscale uses its own secondary replicas), where replicas already exist for HA.

q: A 6 TB database grows by about 100 GB a week and needs near-instant storage growth and snapshot-based backups. A teammate wants to stay on the DTU model to keep billing simple. What should the DBA tell them?
opts: Hyperscale is offered only in the vCore model, so billing must move from DTUs to vCores
Premium DTU tiers switch to Hyperscale storage automatically once the database passes 1 TB
Hyperscale works in either model, but only when Azure Hybrid Benefit is applied
A DTU database can reach Hyperscale only by exporting a BACPAC to a new server
why: Hyperscale is a vCore-model service tier, so the DTU model cannot deliver it and the move means choosing a vCore Hyperscale service objective. DTU Premium has no automatic switch to Hyperscale storage. Hybrid Benefit is a licensing discount and is not a prerequisite for selecting Hyperscale. A BACPAC export is not required because the service objective of an existing database can be changed to vCore Hyperscale.

q: A database will run at a steady eight vCores around the clock for the next three years, and the company holds SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance. Which approach gives the lowest compute cost on Azure SQL Database?
opts: Serverless compute with auto-pause and a high minimum vCore setting
Provisioned vCore compute with a three-year reservation and Azure Hybrid Benefit
A DTU Premium database with a three-year reservation applied
Provisioned vCore compute billed pay-as-you-go to keep commitments flexible
why: A steady, always-on workload gets the deepest discount from reserved capacity on provisioned vCore compute, and Hybrid Benefit stacks on top by removing the license component. Serverless is for intermittent load; with no idle time there is nothing to pause, and per-second billing costs more than a reservation. Reservations apply to vCore compute, not to DTU databases. Pay-as-you-go keeps flexibility the scenario does not need, at the highest unit price.

q: A DBA on a macOS laptop must connect to Azure SQL with Microsoft Entra MFA, keep runbook-style notebooks mixing T-SQL and notes, and run a migration assessment of an on-premises server without maintaining a Windows machine. Which tool fits?
opts: Azure Data Studio with the Azure SQL Migration extension (now retired)
SQL Server Management Studio running locally
The Data Migration Assistant desktop application (retired July 2025)
Azure Storage Explorer with the SQL extension
why: Azure Data Studio runs natively on macOS, supports Entra authentication and notebooks, and its Azure SQL Migration extension performed assessment and migration from the same tool; this wording comes from older exam material, since Azure Data Studio and the extension were retired on February 28, 2026, and the current equivalent is the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code (cross-platform) together with the migration experiences in Azure Arc, Azure Migrate, and Azure Database Migration Service. SSMS and the Data Migration Assistant (itself retired in July 2025) are Windows applications. Azure Storage Explorer manages blob, file, and queue data and has no T-SQL query or migration assessment capability.

q: A Hyperscale named replica can run at a different compute size than the primary, and clients reach it by connecting to its own database name rather than by setting ApplicationIntent.
opts: True
False
why: Named replicas are independently sized readable replicas addressed by their own database name, which is how a reporting workload can be isolated from the primary. High-availability replicas, by contrast, are reached through ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly and cannot be sized independently.

q: Planned platform maintenance caused a brief reconnect during a flash sale. The DBA wants to prevent that from recurring at peak hours. Which statement describes what can be configured?
opts: Choose a maintenance window so planned maintenance is applied in a slot that avoids peak hours
Set a maintenance freeze so platform updates are deferred until the DBA releases them
Enable zone redundancy, since zone-redundant databases are patched without a reconnect
Move to Business Critical, since replicas are patched one at a time with no client impact
why: A maintenance window controls when planned maintenance happens; the events still occur and still cause a brief reconnect, but they land in the chosen slot. There is no indefinite deferral setting. Zone redundancy improves resilience to a zone failure but does not remove maintenance-related reconnects. Business Critical fails over between replicas during maintenance, which also drops connections briefly, so applications still need retry logic.

q: An analyst on a Managed Instance needs ad hoc T-SQL against Parquet files in Azure Data Lake Storage. The files change daily and must not be copied into SQL tables first. Which approach fits?
opts: Define an external data source and query the files with an external table or OPENROWSET
Schedule a BULK INSERT into a staging table each morning
Create elastic query external tables that point at the storage account folder
Add a linked server that targets the storage account's blob endpoint
why: Data virtualization on Managed Instance lets T-SQL read files in storage in place through an external data source plus an external table or OPENROWSET, so the data never has to be loaded. BULK INSERT copies the data, which the scenario prohibits. Elastic query targets other Azure SQL databases, not files in a storage account. A linked server connects to database engines and cannot be pointed at a blob endpoint.

q: A nightly sync job only needs to know which rows were inserted, updated, or deleted since its last run, identified by primary key, so it can re-read current values. Storage and I/O overhead on the source must stay as low as possible. Which feature fits?
opts: Change Data Capture, reading from its change tables
Change Tracking, querying the changes since the last synchronization version
A temporal table, comparing history rows against the current table
Query Store, listing statements that modified the table
why: Change Tracking records only that a row changed and a version number, which is exactly enough to re-fetch current values and carries the smallest overhead. Change Data Capture stores full before and after values in change tables and costs more storage and I/O than this job needs. A temporal table keeps full row history for every change, again far more than required. Query Store records statement and plan statistics, not which rows changed.

q: Enabling Change Data Capture on a table in Azure SQL Database requires SQL Server Agent to be running, because the capture and cleanup jobs are SQL Agent jobs.
opts: True
False
why: SQL Agent does not exist in single-database Azure SQL Database. There, Change Data Capture uses a built-in scheduler to run its capture and cleanup processes. On Managed Instance and SQL Server on a VM the same processes run as SQL Agent jobs, which is the source of the misconception.

q: A team creates a SQL database in Microsoft Fabric for a new line-of-business app. Analysts want to run Spark and Power BI over the same data without building a copy pipeline, and the app team plans to connect with a SQL login and password. Which statement is accurate?
opts: The database works like a Managed Instance, so SQL Agent jobs copy data to OneLake on a schedule
Mirroring must be enabled table by table first, and SQL logins work once a workspace admin turns on SQL authentication
Data is mirrored automatically into OneLake and queried through a read-only SQL analytics endpoint, but connections must use Microsoft Entra authentication, so the SQL login plan must change
Data reaches OneLake only through a nightly pipeline, and SQL logins are managed on a logical server
why: A SQL database in Fabric uses the Azure SQL Database engine, replicates its data into OneLake automatically with no configuration, and exposes it through a read-only SQL analytics endpoint. Like other Fabric items it relies on Microsoft Entra authentication, so SQL logins are not an option. Per-table mirroring setup, nightly pipelines, and SQL Agent copy jobs all describe work the service does for you or features it does not have.

q: A 4 TB sales table on a Managed Instance gets a new month of rows each month, and the oldest month must be removed every month. A DELETE takes hours, bloats the log, and blocks report queries. Which design removes the oldest month in seconds?
opts: Partition the table by month on an aligned scheme, switch the oldest partition out to an identically structured staging table, then truncate that table
Move the table into an elastic pool so the delete gets more resources
Add a nonclustered index on the date column so the delete can seek
Apply PAGE compression to the table so that the delete touches fewer pages
why: Partition switching is a metadata-only operation, so the old month leaves the table instantly and can then be truncated or archived without a long, fully logged delete. Compression shrinks pages but the delete still logs every row. An index helps find rows, not remove them cheaply. An elastic pool is a Database-only resource-sharing model and would not change how deletes are logged.

q: A partition function on a datetime2 column is created with RANGE RIGHT and boundary values of 2026-01-01, 2026-02-01, and 2026-03-01. In which partition does a row stamped 2026-02-01 00:00:00 land?
opts: Partition 1, because only values before the first boundary use the first partition
Partition 2, because the boundary value belongs to the partition on its left
Partition 3, because the February boundary is the lowest value of the partition on its right
It fails, because a row exactly equal to a boundary value must be assigned manually
why: With RANGE RIGHT each boundary value is the inclusive lower bound of the partition to its right: partition 1 holds values below 2026-01-01, partition 2 holds January, partition 3 holds February, and partition 4 holds March onward. With RANGE LEFT the boundary would belong to the partition on its left, which is why RIGHT is preferred for date boundaries. Rows equal to a boundary are always placed automatically.

q: A SaaS provider will host 3,000 tenants in Azure SQL Database, one tenant range per database, and needs a way to route each request to the correct database and to move a heavy tenant's data to another database later. Which approach fits?
opts: An elastic pool alone, since pooled databases are automatically routed by tenant
A partitioned table with one partition per tenant, spread over multiple databases
An auto-failover group that holds one database per tenant range
A shard map from the Elastic Database client library to route requests, with the split-merge tool to move data between shards
why: Sharding spreads identically structured data across separate databases, and the Elastic Database client library's shard map is what resolves a tenant key to a database, while split-merge relocates ranges. A partitioned table cannot span databases because all partitions must reside in the same database. An elastic pool only shares compute and does no routing. A failover group replicates for disaster recovery and has nothing to do with tenant placement.

q: A clustered columnstore fact table has partitions that are almost never read, and the team wants the smallest possible footprint on those cold partitions, accepting higher CPU and slower reads. What should they apply to those partitions?
opts: Columnstore archival compression (COLUMNSTORE_ARCHIVE) on the cold partitions
PAGE compression on the cold partitions
ROW compression on the cold partitions
Wrapping the columns in the COMPRESS function so the values are indexed more tightly
why: Columnstore archival compression is built for exactly this case and can be set per partition, further reducing size at the cost of CPU and read time. ROW and PAGE compression apply to rowstore objects, because columnstore objects always use columnstore compression and that is not user configurable. The COMPRESS function produces GZIP values that cannot be indexed, which makes it a poor fit for table-wide space saving.

q: A DBA starts an online database move between two Managed Instances at 09:00. Seeding finishes by 10:00, the status shows ready for completion, and the DBA forgets about it. What is the state the next morning?
opts: The operation silently converted to a copy, and both databases are online and independent
The operation is still waiting indefinitely, and the destination keeps applying changes from the source
The operation completed itself after seeding, and the source database has been dropped
The operation was cancelled after 24 hours, the destination database was dropped, and the source database is untouched
why: Until a copy or move is explicitly completed, changes keep flowing to the destination, but you have 24 hours to complete it; after that the operation is cancelled automatically and the destination database is dropped. Nothing completes on its own and a move never converts to a copy, so the source is never dropped without an explicit completion.

q: A General Purpose Managed Instance is about to exceed 100 databases and 16 TB of reserved storage. Budget is tight and the workload does not need Business Critical's local SSD and built-in replicas. What is the best change?
opts: Enable the Next-gen General Purpose upgrade on the existing instance
Convert the instance to a DTU-based elastic pool
Move the databases to a Business Critical instance
Split the databases across several General Purpose instances in different virtual networks
why: Next-gen General Purpose is an in-place upgrade that keeps the General Purpose baseline cost and raises limits to up to 500 databases and 32 TB, using Elastic SAN for better IOPS. Business Critical costs more and is aimed at low-latency, high-resiliency needs the scenario excludes. Splitting instances adds management overhead and cost, and a Managed Instance cannot be converted to an elastic pool.

q: A company runs SQL Server 2022 on-premises. For a new Managed Instance it must keep the ability to restore a database from the instance back to SQL Server 2022 and to use the Managed Instance link with it. Which update policy should the instance use?
opts: The SQL Server 2025 update policy
Any policy, because the database format never changes after creation
The Always-up-to-date update policy
The SQL Server 2022 update policy
why: The versioned policies align the internal database format with a specific SQL Server version, so the 2022 policy keeps databases compatible with SQL Server 2022. Always-up-to-date gains new engine features but its format no longer aligns with any on-premises version, and the 2025 policy aligns with 2025, which a 2022 instance cannot restore. The format does differ by policy, which is the whole point of the setting.

q: SQL Server on Azure VMs are patched with the SQL IaaS Agent extension's Automated Patching feature. The team wants cumulative updates installed automatically, and learns that the feature is scheduled for retirement. What should they do?
opts: Move every database to Azure SQL Database, because VMs cannot be patched from Azure
Disable the SQL IaaS Agent extension, since it was the source of patching
Leave Automated Patching on and add automatic VM guest patching as a second safety net
Migrate to Azure Update Manager, and avoid running more than one automatic patching mechanism on the same VM
why: Azure Update Manager is the supported replacement and is the integrated way to install SQL Server cumulative updates, whereas Automated Patching installs only updates marked Important or Critical. Stacking several automatic mechanisms on one VM can cause failed updates. Azure can patch VMs through Update Manager, so migrating to PaaS is unnecessary, and the extension provides other features that the team likely uses.

q: Which two settings follow Microsoft's guidance for the disks of a SQL Server on Azure VM? (Choose two.)
opts: Host caching set to ReadWrite on data and log disks for maximum write speed
Host caching set to None on the disks holding transaction log files
Data, log, and tempdb files placed together on one disk to simplify management
Host caching set to ReadOnly on the disks holding data files
why: Read caching helps data files that are read randomly, while log writes are sequential and gain nothing from caching, so None is right for log disks. ReadWrite caching on data or log disks risks losing writes and is not recommended. Data, log, and tempdb files should be on separate volumes so their I/O patterns do not compete.

q: A SQL Server 2016 instance in a regional office must stay on-premises, but it is out of support. The company wants security updates for it, a central Azure inventory of all its SQL Server instances, and pay-as-you-go billing where possible. What should it use?
opts: Azure Backup for SQL Server on the on-premises server
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale with the database imported as a BACPAC
SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc, with an Extended Security Updates subscription
A Managed Instance link to a Managed Instance in Azure
why: Arc projects the instance into Azure for inventory, assessment, Defender, and pay-as-you-go licensing without moving it, and ESUs can be purchased for out-of-support versions for up to three years. The Managed Instance link replicates to Azure and is a migration or DR tool, not management of the on-premises server. Backup protects data but supplies no patches or inventory, and importing into Hyperscale moves the database off-premises.

q: A team uses Log Replay Service to migrate a database to Managed Instance and cut over, bringing the database online. Later they find one more differential backup that should have been restored. What must they do?
opts: Restore the extra differential directly with RESTORE ... WITH NORECOVERY on the online database
Nothing, because the service restores new files in the folder even after cutover
Start Log Replay Service again against the same database to apply the extra differential
Delete the database from the managed instance and restart the migration from the beginning
why: Once Log Replay Service stops, by autocomplete or manual cutover, the restore process cannot be resumed for a database that has been brought online, so further backups cannot be applied to it. The database has to be removed and the migration restarted. Starting the service on the same online database, restoring over it with NORECOVERY, or expecting continued restores all assume a restoring state that no longer exists.

q: Two months ago a team converted an existing Azure SQL Database to Hyperscale, and it now wants to return to General Purpose because costs are higher than expected. What is true?
opts: Point-in-time restore to a General Purpose database is the supported way back
A service tier change to General Purpose in the portal works because Hyperscale is only a purchasing option
Reverse migration to General Purpose or Business Critical is available at any time
Reverse migration is no longer available because the 45-day window has passed, so export/import or another data movement tool is required
why: Reverse migration from Hyperscale is only available within 45 days of the original conversion, only to General Purpose, and only for databases that were converted rather than created in Hyperscale. Past that window, bulk export/import tools such as BACPAC (for smaller databases), Data Factory, or bulk copy are the way out. Hyperscale is a separate architecture, so an ordinary tier change is not offered, and PITR restores within the same architecture.

q: A database moved from the DTU purchasing model to the vCore model, other than into Hyperscale, can later be moved back to the DTU model using the same steps.
opts: True
False
why: Switching purchasing models is similar to scaling between service objectives and can be repeated in either direction, with minimal downtime at the end. The exception is a database moved to Hyperscale, which cannot go back to the DTU model by this route.

q: Six DBAs need db_owner on one database, and only that one, on a logical server that hosts many databases. Membership changes often. Access must use Microsoft Entra ID with MFA, and a change must not require running T-SQL. What should be configured?
opts: A contained database user for a Microsoft Entra group, added to db_owner in that database
The same Microsoft Entra group set as the server's Microsoft Entra admin
An individual contained user for each DBA, mapped to the DBA's Entra account
One SQL authentication user in the database, with a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA
why: A database user created FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for an Entra group gives group members db_owner in that one database, and adding or removing members happens in Entra ID alone, with MFA. Making the group the server admin grants control of every database on the server, which exceeds the scope. Per-DBA users make every membership change a T-SQL task. Conditional Access applies to Entra sign-ins, not SQL authentication, so a shared SQL user gets no MFA.

q: After failing over to a geo-secondary on a different logical server, on-premises clients get firewall errors, though they connected fine before. The only allow rules were server-level rules on the original server. What prevents this on the next failover with no manual steps during the event?
opts: Re-create the allowed IP ranges as database-level firewall rules, which replicate with the database
Create the server-level rules on the secondary server after each failover
Enable 'Allow Azure services and resources to access this server' on both servers
Add a virtual network rule on the original server for the corporate network
why: Database-level firewall rules live in the database itself and travel with it through geo-replication, so the secondary already allows the same client ranges when it becomes primary. Creating server-level rules after each failover is a manual step performed during an outage. The Azure-services setting admits traffic from Azure, not on-premises addresses. A virtual network rule on the original server does nothing for the secondary server and is not an on-premises IP allow rule.

q: A healthcare app stores diagnosis codes in Azure SQL Database. Auditors require the codes to stay unreadable to the server's own administrators, including sysadmins running ad hoc queries, with decryption possible only in the approved application. Which solution meets this?
opts: Transparent Data Encryption with a customer-managed key held in Azure Key Vault
Dynamic Data Masking, with the UNMASK permission withheld from the DBA team
Always Encrypted, with the column master key stored in Azure Key Vault
Row-Level Security with a block predicate on the diagnosis table
why: Always Encrypted encrypts and decrypts inside the client driver with keys the engine never holds, so a sysadmin's SELECT returns ciphertext and only the approved application, which can reach the column master key, sees plaintext. TDE with a customer-managed key still lets the engine decrypt data for any query, including the DBA's. Masking only alters displayed results and can be bypassed by a privileged user. Row-Level Security limits which rows are visible, not whether column values are encrypted.

q: An auditor asks how files and automated backups of a newly created Azure SQL Database are protected if someone obtained the storage media. The DBA has not configured any encryption. What is the situation?
opts: Nothing needs configuring; TDE is already on for new databases, using a service-managed key
Encryption is off until the DBA runs ALTER DATABASE ... SET ENCRYPTION ON
The DBA first creates a database master key and certificate in master, then enables TDE
Just the columns marked with Always Encrypted are protected, since PaaS storage is not encrypted by default
why: New Azure SQL databases have TDE enabled by default with a service-managed key, so data files and backups are already encrypted at rest and no application change is needed. The ALTER DATABASE step and the master key and certificate setup are on-premises or VM procedures, not needed for PaaS defaults. Always Encrypted protects chosen columns end to end and is not what secures storage media.

q: Call center agents must see only the last four digits of a stored card number, while supervisors see the full value. The stored data and the application queries must not change. Which approach fits?
opts: Always Encrypted with deterministic encryption, giving supervisors access to the column master key
Row-Level Security with a filter predicate that hides rows from agents
A partial() dynamic data mask on the column, with UNMASK granted to supervisors
Column-level DENY SELECT for the agent role on the card number column
why: Dynamic Data Masking with a partial mask returns only the last four digits to users without UNMASK, while supervisors granted UNMASK see the real value; stored data and queries stay unchanged. Always Encrypted needs driver changes and cannot show a partial value to some users. Row-Level Security removes whole rows, not part of a value. A column DENY makes the query fail for agents instead of returning a masked value.

q: In a multi-tenant table, queries must return only the caller's tenant rows, and a tenant's login must also be unable to insert or update rows carrying another tenant's ID. The rules must apply regardless of how the table is accessed. What should be implemented?
opts: A security policy that contains a filter predicate only
Dynamic Data Masking on the TenantId column
A security policy with filter and block predicates
A CHECK constraint that compares TenantId to USER_NAME()
why: A filter predicate silently hides other tenants' rows from reads, while block predicates (such as AFTER INSERT and AFTER UPDATE) reject writes that would create rows for another tenant; both are attached to one security policy. A filter predicate alone leaves writes unchecked. Masking changes how a value displays and restricts nothing. A CHECK constraint cannot filter reads and would apply to all writers, including administrative processes.

q: Azure SQL Auditing already records all statements, yet the security team learned of a SQL injection attempt only from a manual log review. They want automatic alerts at runtime for injection attempts and unusual access patterns. What should be enabled?
opts: Advanced Threat Protection in Microsoft Defender for SQL
SQL Vulnerability Assessment scans on a weekly schedule
Auditing to a Log Analytics workspace with a longer retention period
Dynamic Data Masking on the columns the application queries
why: Advanced Threat Protection watches activity at runtime and raises alerts for suspicious behavior such as injection attempts and anomalous access. Vulnerability Assessment scans configuration against best practices, so it reports weaknesses, not live attacks. Auditing, even to Log Analytics, only records events; nothing evaluates them for malicious patterns unless a detection layer is added. Masking changes displayed values and detects nothing.

q: With Always Encrypted, an application that connects without enabling the column encryption setting on its connection receives the raw ciphertext for protected columns instead of an error.
opts: True
False
why: The driver only encrypts parameters and decrypts results when the column encryption setting is enabled. Without it, queries still run, but protected columns come back as encrypted binary values, which is a frequent first-deployment surprise.

q: Automated backups of an Azure SQL Database with TDE enabled are themselves encrypted, with no separate backup-encryption setup.
opts: True
False
why: TDE encrypts data at the page level, so backups taken from the encrypted database inherit that protection automatically. This is why backup files obtained from storage are unreadable without the TDE protector, even though TDE does nothing for queries against the live database.

q: A user who lacks the UNMASK permission can still sometimes infer a masked column's real values by running queries with WHERE filters against that column.
opts: True
False
why: Dynamic Data Masking masks only the displayed result, while filters and joins still operate on the real values, so a user with SELECT can narrow in on a value through repeated predicates. That is why masking is a convenience layer and not a security boundary.

q: Which two items are required for an application to use Always Encrypted columns? (Choose two.)
opts: A column master key held in a key store such as Azure Key Vault that the client can reach
A supporting client driver with the column encryption setting enabled on the connection
A database master key in the database to protect the column encryption keys
Randomized encryption on every column used in equality joins
TDE enabled first, so Always Encrypted can build on the encrypted files
why: The client must be able to reach the column master key, and its driver must have the column encryption setting on so it encrypts parameters and decrypts results. The engine never holds the keys, so no database master key is involved. Joins and equality comparisons need deterministic encryption, since randomized encryption cannot be compared. TDE is an unrelated at-rest feature with no dependency in either direction.

q: A company wants Transparent Data Encryption for its Azure SQL Database protected by its own key in Azure Key Vault, so it controls rotation and can revoke access. Which requirements apply?
opts: Soft-delete and purge protection on the vault, plus get, wrap, and unwrap rights for the server identity
Export the key from the vault and import it into the master database as a certificate
Create a database master key in master and protect it with a password kept in the vault
Enable Always Encrypted on the logical server so that TDE can borrow the vault's key
why: A customer-managed TDE protector requires the key vault to have soft-delete and purge protection (so a deleted key can be recovered), and the server's identity needs get, wrap, and unwrap permissions on the key. Importing the key into master as a certificate is the on-premises TDE pattern. A database master key protected by a vault password is not how the TDE protector is configured in Azure SQL. Always Encrypted is a separate column-level feature and does not supply the TDE protector.

q: Compliance requires auditing every statement on all 30 databases of a logical server, including databases created later, with logs queryable using KQL. Which configuration fits?
opts: Database-level auditing on each of the 30 databases, writing to a storage account
Server-level auditing with a Log Analytics workspace as the destination
Query Store enabled on each database with the capture mode set to All
Defender for SQL threat detection with alerts sent to the security team
why: A server-level audit policy applies to every database on the server, including new ones, and a Log Analytics destination allows KQL queries over the audit records. Per-database policies would miss future databases unless someone remembers to add them, and a storage account does not support KQL directly. Query Store captures plan and runtime statistics, not an audit trail. Threat detection raises alerts on suspicious activity and is not a complete statement log.

q: Which two statements about Azure SQL Auditing are true? (Choose two.)
opts: If server-level and database-level auditing are both enabled, the database is audited by both policies
Audit logs can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace and analyzed with KQL
A database-level audit policy replaces the server-level policy for that database
Auditing can be configured to deny statements that match a sensitive pattern
Audit records are written to tables inside the audited database
why: Server-level and database-level policies run in parallel, so enabling both produces duplicate audit records for that database, and Log Analytics is a supported destination that supports KQL. A database policy does not override the server policy. Auditing only records and never denies a statement. Destinations are a storage account, Log Analytics, or Event Hub, not the audited database itself.

q: A security policy requires that clients using TLS 1.0 or 1.1 be rejected when connecting to an Azure SQL logical server. Which setting enforces this?
opts: Always Encrypted enabled on the sensitive columns
Transparent Data Encryption with a customer-managed key
A private endpoint for the logical server
The server's minimal TLS version set to 1.2
why: The minimal TLS version setting on the logical server rejects connections that negotiate an older protocol. Always Encrypted protects chosen column values and TDE protects data at rest; neither controls the transport protocol version. A private endpoint changes the network path, but clients on it could still negotiate an older TLS version unless the minimum is set.

q: A database already has TDE enabled. Which two threats is TDE alone NOT designed to stop? (Choose two.)
opts: A sysadmin running an ad hoc SELECT against the live database
An attacker who copies backup files out of the storage account
An application user with SELECT permission reading a sensitive column
Someone attaching the raw data files to another server without the key
Theft of the physical disks from the datacenter
why: TDE encrypts data at rest, but the engine decrypts pages as it reads them into memory, so any authorized query, including a sysadmin's or an application user's, returns plaintext. Copied backups, files attached elsewhere, and stolen disks are exactly the offline-access threats TDE addresses, since they are unreadable without the key. Stopping the first two threats needs access control or Always Encrypted.

q: An audit finding states that password-based SQL logins must not be usable at all against an Azure SQL logical server. A Microsoft Entra admin is already configured. What should be done to satisfy the finding?
opts: Rotate the SQL admin password and store the new value in Azure Key Vault
Enable Microsoft Entra-only authentication on the server
Delete every SQL user from each database and keep only the server admin login
Raise the server's minimal TLS version to 1.2
why: Entra-only authentication disables SQL authentication for the server, so password-based logins, including the SQL admin, cannot connect. Rotating the password still leaves a working SQL login. Deleting database users leaves the server admin login as a SQL-auth path. The TLS setting governs the protocol version and says nothing about which authentication methods are accepted.

q: A DBA used Data Discovery & Classification to label columns holding national ID numbers. The compliance team now wants to know who has queried those labeled columns. Which source provides it?
opts: Azure SQL Auditing, which can include sensitivity labels in its records
Query Store runtime statistics filtered by the labeled columns and users
The Vulnerability Assessment baseline findings for the labeled columns
Dynamic Data Masking rules that list each classified column's readers
why: Classification labels are stored with the database metadata and surface in audit records, so Auditing can show which queries returned labeled data and who ran them. Query Store records plan and performance data, not data sensitivity or user identity. Vulnerability Assessment reports configuration findings. Masking rules control display, they do not record access, and classification does not create them automatically.

q: Which two statements about using a private endpoint for Azure SQL Database are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The server's public network access can be denied while VNet clients keep connecting
DNS must resolve the server name to the private IP, typically through a privatelink private DNS zone
On-premises clients can use it with no network path into the virtual network
It replaces SQL and Entra authentication, so logins are no longer required
It is available only for Managed Instance, which already has a VNet address
why: A private endpoint gives the server a private IP in a VNet, and the public endpoint can be switched off with Deny public network access. Clients must resolve the server FQDN to that private address, which is usually done with a privatelink private DNS zone. On-premises clients still need VPN or ExpressRoute connectivity into the VNet. A private endpoint is a network control and does not replace authentication. It is offered for Azure SQL Database; Managed Instance is deployed inside a VNet by design.

q: A database is geo-replicated to a second logical server. After a failover, applications that authenticate with logins created in the original server's master database can no longer connect. Which approach avoids this going forward?
opts: Use contained database users so authentication travels with the database
Create matching logins on the secondary server with new passwords
Copy the master database from the primary server to the secondary
Re-run CREATE USER in each database after each failover
why: Contained database users authenticate against the database itself, so they replicate and fail over with it and need no server-level login. Logins re-created with new SIDs on the secondary will not match the database users, leaving them orphaned. Azure SQL Database does not let you copy master between servers. Re-running CREATE USER after each failover is a manual step and still depends on a matching login.

q: A security engineer must configure auditing and Defender settings on the logical server using Azure RBAC. They must not create or delete databases, and must not be able to read any table data. Which built-in role fits?
opts: SQL DB Contributor
SQL Server Contributor
SQL Security Manager
The db_owner database role
why: SQL Security Manager manages the security-related policies of SQL servers and databases without granting data access or database lifecycle control. SQL DB Contributor and SQL Server Contributor manage databases and servers but explicitly cannot manage their security policies. db_owner is a SQL database role (data plane), not an Azure RBAC role, and it would grant full data access.

q: Which two statements about Azure RBAC and SQL permissions on Azure SQL Database are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The server's Microsoft Entra admin has administrative access to every database on that server
SQL DB Contributor can create, scale, and delete databases but cannot read table data
Azure Contributor on the subscription makes a user db_owner in every database below it
Membership in db_datareader lets a user change a database's service objective
A Global Administrator in Entra ID is automatically a sysadmin on all logical servers
why: The Entra admin is a data-plane identity with administrative rights across the server's databases, while SQL DB Contributor is a control-plane role that manages database resources without granting access to rows. Azure RBAC roles, even Contributor at subscription scope, do not map to SQL roles. db_datareader is a data-plane role that cannot change the resource. Directory roles such as Global Administrator carry no automatic rights on SQL servers.

q: Always Encrypted columns hold customer names. The team needs LIKE pattern matching on them and wants to encrypt the existing table in place instead of exporting it to a client tool, while DBAs must still never see plaintext outside the engine's protected region. Which feature meets this?
opts: Transparent Data Encryption with a customer-managed key
Always Encrypted with deterministic encryption only
Always Encrypted with secure enclaves, using enclave-enabled keys and attestation
Dynamic Data Masking with a partial mask
why: A secure enclave lets the engine decrypt and compute on encrypted data inside protected memory, which enables in-place encryption and pattern matching while the keys and plaintext stay hidden from administrators outside the enclave. Plain deterministic Always Encrypted supports only equality comparisons. Masking only changes how results look, and TDE encrypts files at rest while the engine and DBAs still see plaintext.

q: Always Encrypted with VBS enclaves requires special processor hardware, such as Intel SGX, in the database's host.
opts: True
False
why: VBS enclaves are software-based, relying on the Windows hypervisor, and need no special hardware. Intel SGX enclaves are the hardware-based type, used on DC-series Azure SQL Database hardware, and their support is scheduled to end on October 31, 2027.

q: Auditors need cryptographic proof that nobody, including DBAs and cloud administrators, has altered rows in an Orders table. The application updates order rows constantly, and every earlier version of a row must be preserved. Which design fits?
opts: A system-versioned temporal table with auditing enabled on the history table
Transparent Data Encryption with a customer-managed key in Key Vault
An append-only ledger table, with the application inserting a new row for every change
An updatable ledger table, with database digests stored in immutable storage
why: An updatable ledger table lets the application keep issuing updates and deletes while the engine preserves each earlier row version in a history table and hashes every transaction into the ledger, with digests in immutable storage giving tamper evidence. An append-only table would reject the application's updates. A temporal table keeps history but gives no cryptographic proof, and TDE protects files at rest, not the integrity of data against privileged users.

q: Why should ledger database digests be uploaded to Azure Blob Storage with a locked immutability policy or to Azure Confidential Ledger rather than kept in a table in the same database?
opts: Digests in the database would be removed by the Query Store cleanup task
The database engine cannot read hashes that are stored in its own tables
Verification compares recomputed hashes to the digests, so the digests must be somewhere a privileged attacker cannot alter them
Ledger verification requires the digests to be encrypted by Always Encrypted first
why: Integrity checks are only as strong as the stored digests: if an administrator who can alter the data could also rewrite the digests, tampering would pass verification. Immutable or confidential storage removes that option. Query Store cleanup is unrelated, Always Encrypted is not a prerequisite, and the engine can read its own tables.

q: A developer must protect a single payment-token column inside the database with built-in T-SQL, using a symmetric key that is itself protected by a certificate. Permissions on the key should decide who can read the value. Which feature is this?
opts: Dynamic Data Masking with a default mask on the column
Column-level encryption using ENCRYPTBYKEY and DECRYPTBYKEY on a varbinary column
A database firewall rule that blocks the column's queries
Row-Level Security with a filter predicate on the column
why: Cell or column encryption with symmetric keys protected by a certificate stores ciphertext in a varbinary column, and only principals with permission to open the key can decrypt it. Masking only changes what non-privileged users see while the stored value stays readable, Row-Level Security filters rows rather than protecting column contents, and firewall rules act on network sources, not columns.

q: Which two statements about Microsoft Entra authentication for SQL Server are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Turning it on disables SQL authentication for the instance
For SQL Server on an Azure VM, the VM is registered with the SQL Server IaaS Agent extension rather than Azure Arc
It requires SQL Server 2022 or later
It also works on SQL Server 2019 once the latest cumulative update is installed
why: Entra authentication was introduced with SQL Server 2022 and is enabled on-premises through Azure Arc registration or on Azure Windows VMs through the SQL IaaS Agent extension. Earlier versions do not support it. It is added alongside SQL and Windows authentication, which remain unchanged; only the Azure SQL Entra-only setting removes SQL logins.

q: A legacy web app on domain-joined servers uses Windows Authentication with Kerberos double-hop impersonation and cannot be rewritten. After moving its database to Azure SQL Managed Instance, it must keep working without deploying Microsoft Entra Domain Services. What should the team configure?
opts: Microsoft Entra-only authentication on the instance
A private endpoint that restricts the instance to the web servers' subnet
Windows Authentication for Microsoft Entra principals using Entra Kerberos
SQL authentication with a shared login for the application
why: Windows Authentication for Entra principals lets AD-, Entra-, or hybrid-joined clients use Kerberos, including double-hop patterns, against Managed Instance with no code change and no Domain Services. Entra-only authentication disables SQL logins and requires Entra-based connections. A shared SQL login discards per-user identity and impersonation, and a private endpoint controls network reachability, not the authentication protocol.

q: A report query became slower sometime in the last week, and the database failed over twice in that period. The DBA needs per-plan runtime history to see when the plan changed. Which source can provide it?
opts: Query Store runtime statistics for the query
sys.dm_exec_query_stats filtered on the query hash
An Extended Events session created today
sys.dm_db_resource_stats, reviewed for the same week
why: Query Store persists plans and runtime statistics inside the database, so history survives failovers and shows when a different plan began. sys.dm_exec_query_stats reads the plan cache, which is rebuilt after a failover, so older data is gone. A session created today captures nothing from earlier in the week. sys.dm_db_resource_stats covers about the last hour of database-level utilization and has no per-query or per-plan detail.

q: Deadlocks occur sporadically in an Azure SQL Database, and the DBA needs the deadlock graphs captured going forward and kept after restarts and failovers. Which approach fits?
opts: SQL Server Profiler with the Deadlock Graph event, run from the DBA's workstation
An Extended Events session capturing xml_deadlock_report, written to an event_file target in Azure Storage
An Extended Events session with a ring_buffer target alone, queried when a deadlock is reported
Query Store's Top Resource Consuming Queries view, reviewed after each incident
why: An Extended Events session for xml_deadlock_report records each deadlock graph, and an event_file target in Azure Storage keeps them durably. Profiler cannot connect to Azure SQL Database. A ring_buffer target lives in memory, so events are lost on restart or failover. Query Store ranks resource consumers and records no deadlock graphs.

q: Users report a database was slow for about 20 minutes three days ago. The DBA wants CPU, data I/O, and log I/O percentages for that window. Which source should be queried?
opts: sys.dm_db_resource_stats in the user database
sys.resource_stats in the logical server's master database
sys.dm_exec_query_stats in the user database
sys.dm_db_missing_index_details in the user database
why: sys.resource_stats in master keeps roughly 14 days of utilization at 5-minute granularity, which covers a window three days back. sys.dm_db_resource_stats has finer 15-second data but retains only about an hour. sys.dm_exec_query_stats reports cached-plan statistics per query, not database utilization percentages. The missing index DMV lists index suggestions.

q: A team wants automatic root-cause analysis of performance degradations, such as a regressed plan or lock contention, written as diagnostic records they can analyze or forward to a SIEM, without writing monitoring queries. What should they configure?
opts: Query Store with capture mode All, plus a scheduled export of its catalog views to storage
The SQLInsights log category in diagnostic settings, streamed to Log Analytics
A Query Performance Insight dashboard pinned to the team's portal and shared with the SIEM team
Server-level auditing with an Event Hub destination feeding the SIEM
why: Intelligent Insights emits its findings as the SQLInsights log category, which a diagnostic setting streams to Log Analytics, Event Hubs, or storage for analysis or SIEM forwarding. Query Store collects the raw plan data but does not diagnose causes by itself. Query Performance Insight visualizes top queries without producing diagnostic records. Auditing records executed statements, not performance diagnoses.

q: A DBA wants an email whenever a database's CPU percentage averages above 90% over 10 minutes. No diagnostic settings are configured for the database. Which approach works?
opts: A log alert running a KQL query against a Log Analytics workspace every few minutes
An Azure Monitor metric alert on CPU percentage, with an action group that emails the team
A SQL Agent alert on a performance condition, paired with a Database Mail profile
An audit action group configured to fire when CPU-heavy statements are logged
why: Platform metrics such as CPU percentage flow to Azure Monitor automatically, so a metric alert with an email action group works without diagnostic settings. A KQL log alert needs resource logs sent to Log Analytics through a diagnostic setting first. SQL Agent does not exist on Azure SQL Database single databases. Auditing is not an alerting mechanism and there is no audit action group.

q: If Query Store reaches its maximum storage size and cleanup cannot free space, it switches to read-only and stops recording new queries.
opts: True
False
why: Query Store changes its actual state to read-only when its size cap is reached, so existing history stays readable but new plans and statistics are not captured. A DBA who sees stale data should check the actual state against the desired state, then raise the size limit or enable size-based cleanup.

q: SSMS's XEvent Profiler relies on SQL Trace, so like SQL Server Profiler it cannot capture live events from an Azure SQL Database.
opts: True
False
why: XEvent Profiler only looks like Profiler: it is built on Extended Events sessions, which Azure SQL Database supports, so it can display live events there. The legacy Profiler and SQL Trace depend on a trace mechanism that Azure SQL Database does not expose.

q: Which two statements about Query Store in Azure SQL Database are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It is enabled by default on new databases
It can record wait statistics per query plan
It captures only SELECT statements
A forced plan is guaranteed to be used even if the index it needs is dropped
Its data is stored in the master database of the logical server
why: Query Store is on by default in Azure SQL Database and, with wait statistics capture, can attribute waits to a plan. It records data-modification and other statements as well as SELECTs. Plan forcing fails if the plan depends on an object that no longer exists, and the optimizer then compiles normally. Its data lives in the user database itself, not in master.

q: A DBA finds many sessions in sys.dm_exec_requests with a LCK_M_X wait type and a nonzero blocking_session_id, while CPU stays low. What is the right next step?
opts: Scale up to more vCores, since lock waits indicate compute pressure
Follow blocking_session_id to the head blocker and inspect its text and open transaction
Check sys.dm_db_missing_index_details for the tables involved and create the suggested indexes
KILL the sessions that show a LCK_M_X wait, to clear the queue
why: Lock waits chain back to a head blocker, often a long-running or abandoned open transaction, and finding it is the way to fix blocking. More vCores do not shorten lock waits, and CPU is low anyway. Creating every suggested index is not a response to blocking and has its own cost. Killing the waiting sessions kills the victims rather than the blocker, so the queue refills.

q: In Azure SQL Database, an Extended Events session is created at the database level, not the server level.
opts: True
False
why: Because a logical server hosts independent databases, sessions are created with ON DATABASE and capture events for that database only. The server-scoped sessions familiar from on-premises SQL Server exist on Managed Instance and SQL Server on a VM.

q: A Standard-tier database shows 100% DTU consumption in the portal. sys.dm_db_resource_stats shows avg_cpu_percent near 20, avg_data_io_percent near 15, and avg_log_write_percent near 100. What should the DBA conclude?
opts: Log write throughput is the limiting dimension, so find the heavy write statements before choosing a resize
CPU is the limiting dimension, so move to a tier with more compute
Data I/O is the limiting dimension, so add a nonclustered index on each table
The database is healthy, because DTU percentage is the average of the three resource percentages
why: DTU consumption reflects the highest of the CPU, data I/O, and log I/O percentages, so 100% DTU with only log writes at 100% means log throughput is the cap. Finding the statements that generate the log volume, for example with Query Store, may remove the need to resize at all. CPU and data I/O are far from their limits. DTU percentage is the maximum, not the average, so the database is not healthy.

q: The Query Performance Insight blade for a database shows no data even though users are running queries. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Diagnostic settings have not been configured to send logs to Log Analytics
Query Store is off or read-only, so no query data is being captured
Intelligent Insights has not been enabled for the logical server's databases
Server-level auditing has not been enabled for the logical server
why: Query Performance Insight is a visualization over Query Store, so if Query Store is off or has gone read-only, there is nothing to chart. It does not read diagnostic-setting logs. Intelligent Insights is a separate diagnostic feature that the blade does not depend on. Auditing records statements for review and plays no part in the blade.

q: Unlike ordinary blocking, a deadlock never resolves by itself: both sessions wait until a DBA kills one of them.
opts: True
False
why: The engine detects deadlocks and picks a victim, rolling back its transaction and returning error 1205 so the other session can proceed. Ordinary blocking is the case that persists until the blocker commits, rolls back, or is killed.

q: On a Managed Instance, a reporting login's ad hoc queries occasionally consume enough CPU to slow the OLTP workload sharing the instance. The DBA wants to cap the reporting workload. What should be configured?
opts: A CPU-capped resource pool, a workload group, and a classifier routing the login
A database-scoped MAXDOP of 1 on the database that holds the reporting data
Query Store forced plans applied to each of the reporting queries
A lowered max server memory setting applied to the whole managed instance
why: Resource Governor on Managed Instance caps a workload by combining a resource pool, a workload group, and a classifier function that assigns the reporting login to that group. MAXDOP limits parallelism per query for everyone using that database, not the login's total CPU share. Forced plans pick plan shapes, not resource caps. Lowering instance memory hurts the OLTP workload as well.

q: A plan forced through Query Store is held in the plan cache, so the forcing is lost after a failover.
opts: True
False
why: Forced-plan information is stored in the Query Store inside the database, so it persists across restarts and failovers. The plan cache is volatile, which is the property that makes DMVs such as sys.dm_exec_query_stats unreliable for history.

q: An organization runs 300 Azure SQL databases and several Managed Instances and wants agentless, in-depth monitoring with portal dashboards and alerts across the whole estate. Collected data must be stored in its own subscription and queryable with KQL. Which service should it use?
opts: Query Performance Insight on each database
Intelligent Insights alone, since it stores history for all databases
Database watcher, with an Azure Data Explorer or Fabric Real-Time Analytics data store
SQL Server Profiler traces saved to a file share
why: Database watcher needs no agents, collects performance, configuration, and health data from the chosen databases, pools, and instances into an Azure Data Explorer or Fabric Real-Time Analytics store, and offers dashboards and alerts. Query Performance Insight is a per-database blade, Profiler cannot connect to Azure SQL Database, and Intelligent Insights emits diagnostic records about detected degradations rather than an estate-wide data store.

q: Which two statements about database watcher are true? (Choose two.)
opts: An administrator grants the watcher's managed identity limited access on each SQL target by running T-SQL
A monitoring agent must be installed on every monitored database server
It supports Azure SQL Database only and cannot monitor Managed Instances
Monitoring data is stored in an Azure Data Explorer or Real-Time Analytics database that you own
why: A watcher writes to a data store in your subscription and reads each target through its managed identity, which an administrator authorizes with T-SQL grants. It is agentless, and it supports both Azure SQL Database (including pools and Hyperscale) and Azure SQL Managed Instance.

q: A DBA must decide whether a 70% CPU reading on a production database is abnormal. No historical data was kept. What should the team put in place to answer this kind of question in future?
opts: Capture CPU, I/O, waits, and Query Store runtime statistics on a schedule over a representative period and keep them in Log Analytics or a watcher data store
Take one snapshot at the busiest moment and compare every future reading with it
Track only CPU percentage from the portal's current view
Clear the Query Store regularly so only the latest plans remain visible
why: A baseline needs several metrics sampled repeatedly across normal and peak periods and retained somewhere durable, so a reading can be judged against typical behavior. A single peak snapshot is unrepresentative, CPU alone hides I/O and wait problems, and clearing Query Store throws away the history that makes plan regressions visible.

q: On a Hyperscale database, a DBA wants an integrity check of a critical table, and DBCC CHECKDB is not available. Which command is the documented alternative?
opts: ALTER DATABASE SET PAGE_VERIFY CHECKSUM
DBCC SHRINKDATABASE on the database
DBCC CHECKDB with REPAIR_REBUILD
DBCC CHECKTABLE on the table with the TABLOCK option
why: For Hyperscale, Microsoft documents DBCC CHECKTABLE ... WITH TABLOCK for individual tables as the alternative. CHECKDB is the command that is unavailable, REPAIR options are not usable by customers in Azure SQL Database, page verification is always CHECKSUM and is not a manual integrity check, and shrinking has nothing to do with integrity.

q: In Azure SQL Database, a DBA can run DBCC CHECKDB with REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS to fix corruption that a check reports.
opts: True
False
why: Repair options require single-user mode, which Azure SQL Database does not allow. Microsoft engineers can perform repairs with the customer's approval, and the usual customer recovery is point-in-time restore to a point before the damage. Even on SQL Server, restoring from a known good backup is preferred over REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS.

q: Mornings after an overnight bulk load, a report query is slow. Its actual plan shows 50 estimated rows but 500,000 actual rows leaving a join. The query runs ad hoc with no cached-plan reuse. Which action should the DBA take first?
opts: Update statistics on the tables touched by the load, then re-check the plan
Rebuild every index on the affected tables to refresh the plans
Add OPTION (MAXDOP 1) to the query to avoid parallel row skew
Scale the database to a larger compute size
why: A large estimate-versus-actual gap right after a bulk load usually means the statistics describe the old data, so refreshing them lets the optimizer cost the join correctly. Rebuilding indexes does refresh index statistics but is far heavier and does not cover column statistics. MAXDOP changes parallelism, not cardinality estimates. A bigger compute size runs the same bad plan faster at best and treats the symptom.

q: A DBA suspects a heavily updated table carries nonclustered indexes that add write cost but have not been read since the last restart. Which DMV shows seeks, scans, and lookups next to updates for each index?
opts: sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats
sys.dm_exec_cached_plans
why: sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats reports user_seeks, user_scans, user_lookups, and user_updates per index, so indexes with many updates and no reads stand out as drop candidates. The missing index group stats DMV suggests indexes that do not exist yet. sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats measures fragmentation and page density. sys.dm_exec_cached_plans lists plans in the cache and carries no per-index usage counts.

q: A team wants Azure to create beneficial indexes automatically and to revert regressed plans. Their workloads run on Azure SQL Database and on a Managed Instance. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Both options are available on SQL Database, while Managed Instance supports only automatic plan correction
Both options work identically on SQL Database and Managed Instance
Plan correction needs Intelligent Insights enabled first, while index management needs nothing
Automatic index creation applies only after a DBA approves each index in the portal
why: Automatic tuning on SQL Database can create and drop indexes and force the last good plan, but on Managed Instance only FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN is supported. The platforms are therefore not identical. Plan correction relies on Query Store data, not on Intelligent Insights. Automatic index creation is applied without per-index approval when the option is on, and it verifies the result afterward.

q: A vendor application, whose code cannot be modified, runs a stored procedure thousands of times a minute. Occasionally an unusual parameter value leaves a poor plan cached for later calls. Which fix works without editing the procedure and without per-call compilation?
opts: Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the statement inside the procedure
Add OPTIMIZE FOR hints inside the procedure body
Force a known-good plan, or apply a hint, through Query Store
Clear the plan cache each time the report runs
why: Query Store plan forcing or a Query Store hint is applied from the database side to the query, so the unmodifiable vendor code stays as is and no compile cost is added per call. Adding RECOMPILE and OPTIMIZE FOR both mean editing the procedure, and RECOMPILE would also compile thousands of times a minute. Clearing the cache only resets the sniffing lottery for the next first call and hurts every other query.

q: Suggestions in the missing index DMVs are discarded when the database restarts, so an empty result shortly after a restart does not prove that no useful indexes are missing.
opts: True
False
why: The missing index DMVs are in-memory and reset on restart (and when table metadata changes), so they reflect only the workload seen since then. The same limitation, along with the fact that they suggest single indexes, is why their output needs a DBA's judgment.

q: Which two approaches legitimately mitigate a parameter-sniffing problem? (Choose two.)
opts: Use OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN so the plan is built from average density statistics
Force a stable plan for the query in Query Store
Rebuild every index on the table so cached plans are re-created
Disable AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS so plans stay stable between executions
why: OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN avoids tailoring the plan to the first sniffed value, and forcing a stable plan in Query Store pins a generally good plan. Rebuilding indexes invalidates plans once, after which the next first call re-sniffs and the problem returns. Disabling automatic statistics updates leaves the optimizer with stale estimates and makes plans worse in general, not more stable.

q: An orders table serves OLTP traffic with point lookups and frequent updates, but dashboard queries also aggregate a few columns across millions of rows. The team wants faster aggregates without a separate analytics store and without hurting transactional performance. What should they add?
opts: Convert the table to a clustered columnstore index
A filtered nonclustered rowstore index on the order date
A full-text index on the aggregated columns
A nonclustered columnstore index on the aggregated columns
why: A nonclustered columnstore index adds a compressed columnar copy of just the needed columns beside the rowstore, giving fast scans for real-time operational analytics while the clustered rowstore keeps serving lookups and updates. Making the whole table clustered columnstore penalizes point lookups and frequent updates. A filtered rowstore index helps selective seeks, not wide aggregations. Full-text indexing is for word search over text.

q: In Query Store, query_id 5 has two plans: plan_id 12 performs well and the newer plan_id 19 regressed. Which statement forces the better plan without changing the application?
opts: EXEC sp_query_store_unforce_plan @query_id = 5, @plan_id = 12;
EXEC sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 5, @plan_id = 12;
EXEC sp_query_store_remove_plan @plan_id = 12;
DBCC FREEPROCCACHE with the plan_handle of plan 12;
why: sp_query_store_force_plan takes the query and plan identifiers and makes the optimizer use that plan for the query. The unforce procedure does the opposite. sp_query_store_remove_plan deletes the good plan's stored history rather than forcing it. DBCC FREEPROCCACHE evicts a cached plan and forces nothing, so the next compile may pick the bad plan again.

q: In a busy OLTP database, the top wait type by total wait time is WRITELOG. What does this most directly point to?
opts: Queries waiting on locks held by the open transactions of other sessions
Queries waiting for time on a CPU scheduler because compute is saturated
Transactions waiting for log records to be hardened to storage at commit
Queries waiting for memory grants before they can start sorts or hashes
why: WRITELOG is time spent waiting for the log buffer to be flushed to disk at commit, which indicates log write throughput or latency is the limiting factor. Lock waits appear as LCK_M_* types, CPU scheduler pressure typically shows as SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD, and memory-grant waits show as RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE, so each of those other readings corresponds to a different wait type.

q: A Business Critical database's hot inventory-counters table suffers latch and lock contention from thousands of tiny concurrent updates per second. The access code can be rewritten as T-SQL procedures. Which feature targets this?
opts: A memory-optimized table with natively compiled procedures
A clustered columnstore index created on the counters table
Read scale-out for the sessions that perform the updates
Page compression applied to the table's clustered index
why: In-Memory OLTP uses lock-free, latch-free structures and natively compiled procedures, which is aimed at exactly this high-concurrency contention on a hot table. Columnstore speeds analytic scans, not tiny concurrent updates. Read scale-out only routes read-only connections to a replica, so update sessions still run on the primary. Page compression saves storage and I/O but does nothing for lock and latch contention.

q: Which two statements about resumable index rebuilds are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A resumable rebuild requires the operation to run online
While paused, the partially built index keeps consuming disk space until the operation resumes or is aborted
A paused rebuild can be resumed only from the session that started it
Pausing discards the work done so far, so the resume begins from the start
why: RESUMABLE = ON works only with ONLINE = ON, and the partially built index remains on disk, taking space, while the operation is paused. A paused operation can be resumed from any session with ALTER INDEX ... RESUME, and its progress is kept, which is the entire point of the feature.

q: A database migrated to Azure SQL Database still runs at compatibility level 110. The team wants the current optimizer and intelligent query processing features, but any regressed query must be recoverable individually. What is the safest approach?
opts: Raise the level in one step and disable Query Store to avoid its overhead
Turn on Query Store, capture a baseline, raise the level, then force the old plan for any regressed query
Keep level 110 permanently, because migrated databases cannot run at a higher level
Export a BACPAC and import it, which resets the optimizer to the newest behavior
