why: Capturing a Query Store baseline before the change gives each query a known-good plan to compare with and force back if the new level regresses it, so the upgrade is reversible per query. Raising the level with Query Store off removes the safety net. Migrated databases can be raised to the current level. An export and import does not change the compatibility level, which is a property set on the database.

q: After a compatibility level upgrade, one query in one database regressed because of the new cardinality estimator, while other queries benefit from it. The application code cannot be changed. What is the narrowest fix?
opts: Set LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION to ON in the database-scoped configuration
Lower the compatibility level of the database to the previous value
A Query Store hint on that query that forces the legacy estimator
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the application's query text
why: A Query Store hint attaches USE HINT('FORCE_LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION') to just that query without editing the application, leaving every other query on the new estimator. The database-scoped setting and lowering compatibility level both change behavior for all queries in the database. OPTION (RECOMPILE) would require editing the query text and does not select a different estimator.

q: Which two statements about statistics maintenance in Azure SQL are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Automatic updates trigger when enough rows change, and on newer compatibility levels the threshold scales with table size
UPDATE STATISTICS with FULLSCAN can replace sampled statistics with ones built from every row
With AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC on, the query that triggers the update waits for it to finish
A bulk load always refreshes statistics immediately as part of the load
why: Automatic updates fire after a row-modification threshold that, at newer compatibility levels, grows with table size, and FULLSCAN replaces the default sampled statistics with a full-table read. With the asynchronous setting the triggering query does not wait and compiles with the old statistics. A bulk load does not refresh statistics on its own, which is how stale statistics appear right after large loads.

q: A migrated Azure SQL Database runs at compatibility level 130. Queries calling scalar user-defined functions are slow, and a reporting query over rowstore tables would benefit from batch processing without adding columnstore indexes. What is the lowest level that enables both scalar UDF inlining and batch mode on rowstore?
opts: 130, since both are always on in Azure SQL
why: Scalar UDF inlining and batch mode on rowstore both arrive at compatibility level 150. Level 140 brings adaptive joins, interleaved execution, and batch-mode memory grant feedback but not these two. Level 160 adds features such as Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization and is higher than needed. They are not available at 130.

q: Which two intelligent query processing features require database compatibility level 160 in Azure SQL Database? (Choose two.)
opts: Scalar UDF inlining
Interleaved execution for multi-statement table-valued functions
Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization
Degree of parallelism (DOP) feedback
why: Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization, cardinality estimation feedback, and DOP feedback start at level 160, and DOP feedback also needs Query Store enabled. Scalar UDF inlining starts at level 150, and interleaved execution starts at level 140.

q: A team moving to Azure SQL Database finds SQL Server Agent missing. Their nightly jobs only run T-SQL against 12 databases across 3 logical servers. They want job definitions in one central place, with no new virtual machine and no additional database engine instance to buy. What should they use?
opts: Elastic Database Jobs, with a job agent and a target group that covers the servers
SQL Agent on a Managed Instance, connecting to each database through linked servers
Windows Task Scheduler on a small Azure VM that runs sqlcmd for each database
A scheduled-query alert rule in Azure Monitor that executes the maintenance script
why: Elastic Database Jobs is the PaaS-native scheduler for T-SQL across many databases and servers, with definitions stored centrally in a job database. SQL Agent on Managed Instance would work technically but means buying and running another instance, which the scenario excludes. Task Scheduler needs the virtual machine the team does not want. A scheduled-query alert evaluates data and sends notifications; it does not run T-SQL maintenance against the databases.

q: An Elastic Database Job targets a target group made of a logical server. Every execution fails against every database with a login error, though the job definition and schedule are fine. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The job credential maps to no login or user with permissions in the targets
The job agent and the target databases sit in different Azure regions
The SQL Server Agent service on the logical server has stopped
A target group may hold individual databases or pools, but not a logical server
why: Elastic jobs connect to each target with database-scoped credentials, so the corresponding identity must exist, with the needed permissions, in master and in every target database; a missing login fails every target at once. A job agent can target databases in other regions. SQL Agent does not exist for Azure SQL Database, so there is no service to stop. A logical server is a valid target group member and expands to the databases on it.

q: An Azure Automation runbook must run T-SQL maintenance against an Azure SQL Database every night, unattended, with no stored passwords or client secrets to rotate. Which authentication approach fits?
opts: A SQL authentication login whose password is stored as an encrypted Automation variable
The Automation account's managed identity, created as a Microsoft Entra user in the database
A Microsoft Entra user account with MFA enforced, signing in interactively at run time
A service principal whose client secret is kept in the runbook's parameters
why: A managed identity is issued tokens by Azure with no secret for anyone to store or rotate, and creating it as an Entra user in the database grants it only the permissions assigned. The encrypted variable still holds a password that must be rotated. An MFA-enforced account cannot complete an interactive prompt in an unattended job. A service principal secret is still a credential that expires and must be protected.

q: A team must provision the same logical server, database, firewall rules, and auditing settings in dev, test, and production, and be able to re-run the deployment safely at any time to correct configuration drift. Which approach fits best?
opts: A documented portal checklist that each environment owner follows
A Bicep template under source control, deployed by a pipeline
SSMS Generate Scripts output, run against each environment
An Elastic Database Job that issues the CREATE statements nightly
why: A declarative Bicep or ARM template describes the desired state of the Azure resources, so redeploying is idempotent and corrects drift, and the file is version-controlled. A portal checklist is manual and drifts. The SSMS Generate Scripts wizard produces T-SQL for schema objects inside a database, not the Azure resources around it. An elastic job runs T-SQL inside databases and cannot create the logical server or its firewall and auditing configuration.

q: If a job's target group contains a logical server, the job runs only against the databases that existed when the target group was defined.
opts: True
False
why: A server or pool member in a target group is expanded to its databases each time the job runs, so databases created later are picked up without editing anything. Only individually listed databases are fixed at definition time.

q: In a traditional (non-contained) availability group, a SQL Agent job created on the primary replica also exists on the secondaries, so it keeps running after a failover.
opts: True
False
why: Jobs live in msdb, which is not part of the availability group's replicated databases, so a job must be created on every replica, often with logic that checks which replica is primary. Contained availability groups in newer SQL Server versions can replicate jobs, but a traditional group does not.

q: A team wants an Azure Automation runbook to start the moment a specific Azure Monitor metric alert fires, directly and without building custom polling. What should they configure?
opts: An Elastic Database Job that checks the metric every minute and starts the runbook
A SQL Agent alert tied to a performance condition on the database
An Automation Runbook action in the alert's action group
A Logic App that polls the metrics API on a one-minute recurrence
why: An action group can call an Automation runbook directly, so the alert triggers it as soon as it fires with no additional plumbing. An elastic job or a polling Logic App would duplicate the alert evaluation, add latency, and need their own maintenance. A SQL Agent alert reacts to engine conditions, does not exist on single databases, and is not connected to an Azure Monitor alert.

q: A maintenance job must run on every database on a logical server, including databases created later, except one legacy database named LegacyDb. How should the target group be defined?
opts: A server member, plus an excluded database member for LegacyDb
An elastic pool member for the pool that holds most of the databases
Individual database members for each current database except LegacyDb
Two jobs: one on the server and one that reverses the changes on LegacyDb
why: Target groups support exclusion, so a server member covers current and future databases while an excluded database member removes LegacyDb from the expansion. Targeting a pool covers only that pool's databases. Listing databases individually misses any database created later. Running a second job to undo changes on LegacyDb still executes the script there first and invites errors.

q: On a Managed Instance, a DBA wants an email to a distribution list when a nightly SQL Agent maintenance job fails. Which configuration achieves this?
opts: A Database Mail profile and a SQL Agent operator, with the job set to notify the operator on failure
An Azure Monitor action group attached directly to the SQL Agent job step
SMTP settings configured on an Elastic Job agent that is linked to the instance
An Event Grid subscription on the managed instance resource that emails on job failure
why: SQL Agent job notifications use an operator, which delivers mail through Database Mail, so the profile, operator, and failure notification together produce the email. Action groups belong to Azure Monitor alert rules, not to job steps. Elastic Job agents serve single databases and are not linked to a Managed Instance's SQL Agent. Event Grid publishes resource-level events and does not emit SQL Agent job outcomes.

q: An Azure Monitor alert can fire on a specific T-SQL error number with no diagnostic settings configured, because errors are exposed as platform metrics.
opts: True
False
why: Platform metrics cover resource consumption such as CPU, storage, and deadlocks, not individual error numbers. Alerting on a specific error requires the Errors log category sent through a diagnostic setting to Log Analytics and a log alert. On Managed Instance, a SQL Agent alert can react to an error number directly.

q: The DBA team wants a warning when a Managed Instance's used storage passes 85% of its reserved size, early enough to scale before the instance runs out of space. Which approach fits?
opts: An Azure Monitor metric alert on the instance's storage space used metric
A SQL Agent alert on error 1105, raised when a filegroup is full, paired with Database Mail
An Extended Events session on file-growth events, reviewed weekly
A long-term retention policy on each database in the instance
why: A metric alert on storage used evaluates a threshold continuously and notifies through an action group while there is still headroom. A SQL Agent alert on error 1105 fires only after space has already run out, which is too late for a warning. A weekly review of file-growth events is not alerting. Long-term retention governs backup copies and says nothing about instance storage.

q: A DBA wants to define an Elastic Database Job using only T-SQL from SSMS, since the Azure portal has no job designer. Where should they connect and what should they run?
opts: The job database, calling jobs.sp_add_job and jobs.sp_add_jobstep
The logical server's master database, calling msdb.dbo.sp_add_job
Any target database, creating the job with the dbo.sp_add_job procedure there
The SQL Server Agent node in Object Explorer connected to the logical server
why: Elastic jobs are stored in a job database and created with its jobs schema procedures such as jobs.sp_add_job and jobs.sp_add_jobstep (or equivalent PowerShell). Azure SQL Database has no msdb to hold SQL Agent jobs, a target database is not where the job definition lives, and there is no SQL Server Agent node for a logical server.

q: An Elastic Database Job step can execute a PowerShell script block against each target database, the way a SQL Agent PowerShell job step runs on a VM.
opts: True
False
why: Elastic job steps run T-SQL against targets, and there is no PowerShell job step type. Work that needs PowerShell, such as changing a service objective, belongs in an Azure Automation runbook or a pipeline that calls Azure Resource Manager.

q: As part of a scheduled disaster-recovery drill, a script must fail over an Azure SQL Database auto-failover group to the secondary region without losing any committed data. Which command should it run?
opts: Switch-AzSqlDatabaseFailoverGroup, as a planned failover
Switch-AzSqlDatabaseFailoverGroup with the -AllowDataLoss parameter
Invoke-AzSqlDatabaseFailover on the primary database
Remove-AzSqlDatabaseSecondary on the secondary database
why: A planned failover through Switch-AzSqlDatabaseFailoverGroup synchronizes the secondary first, so no committed data is lost and the roles swap cleanly. The -AllowDataLoss variant is a forced failover for real outages and may drop unreplicated transactions. Invoke-AzSqlDatabaseFailover fails over the HA replica within the same region and does not test the cross-region path. Remove-AzSqlDatabaseSecondary breaks the replication relationship instead of failing over.

q: Before running a Bicep deployment against production, a team wants a list of exactly which resources would be created, modified, or deleted, without changing anything. Which operation provides that?
opts: A deployment in complete mode against a test copy of the resource group
A validate operation, such as az deployment group validate
A what-if operation, such as az deployment group what-if
Reading the deployment history of the resource group
why: What-if compares the template to the current state and reports the planned changes, without deploying. Validate only checks that the template and parameters are valid and does not show the change set. Complete mode actually deletes resources missing from the template, and deployment history reports past runs, not future effects.

q: A scheduled ARM template deployment of a logical server, database, and firewall rules failed overnight. Where does the DBA look first to see which resource failed and with what error?
opts: The sys.dm_exec_requests view in the master database
The database's Query Store runtime statistics
The server's SQL auditing log in the storage account
The resource group's Deployments blade and its deployment operations, plus the Activity log
why: Deployment operations record the status and error for each resource a deployment tried to create, and the Activity log holds the matching control-plane events. Query Store, SQL auditing, and request DMVs describe activity inside an existing database, not Azure Resource Manager operations.

q: A nightly SQL Server Agent job on a Managed Instance shows Failed, but the job-level history message is only a short summary. How does the DBA find the actual error?
opts: Look at the Query Store top resource consumers report for the time of the run
Query sys.dm_db_resource_stats for the job's execution window
Re-run the job with a different owner, since errors are not recorded in history
Open the job history with step details expanded, check the failing step's message, and review its output file and the Agent error log
why: Job history stores a summary row for the job and detailed rows per step, where the real error text lives, and step output files and the Agent error log add more context. Resource statistics and Query Store show database workload, not Agent step errors. Changing the owner is a possible fix for permission problems but not a way to find the cause.

q: The compute node hosting a General Purpose vCore database fails. No geo-replication or failover group is configured. How is availability restored?
opts: A local readable secondary replica is promoted, as in the Business Critical tier
Compute is re-created on another node and reattached to the database's remote storage
An active geo-replication secondary in the paired region is promoted automatically
The most recent point-in-time backup is restored to a new database
why: General Purpose separates compute from remote storage that already holds redundant copies, so recovery is a new compute node attaching to the same storage, with a brief outage. Local readable replicas are a Business Critical design and do not exist in General Purpose. Nothing is promoted from a geo-secondary unless one was configured, and restoring a backup is a manual recovery for data loss, not the built-in node-failure path.

q: A regional outage hits. The auto-failover group uses an automatic failover policy with a one-hour grace period, but the business will not wait for the grace period to expire. What can the DBA do?
opts: Initiate a forced failover on the group, accepting that unreplicated transactions may be lost
Initiate a planned failover, which completes with no data loss even while the primary is down
Delete the failover group and recreate it with the secondary server as the primary
Restore the latest backup in the secondary region, then fail over the restored copy
why: A forced failover (the allow-data-loss option) promotes the secondary immediately, trading possible loss of transactions not yet replicated for faster recovery. A planned failover first synchronizes the secondary with the primary, which cannot happen while the primary is unreachable. Deleting and recreating the group does not promote anything and removes the stable listener. Restoring a backup is slower and the restored copy would not be part of the group.

q: A single large database needs readable copies in three different regions for local reporting, and any failover must remain an administrator's decision. Which configuration fits?
opts: An auto-failover group that lists all three regional servers as secondaries
Read scale-out on the primary, replicated to the three regions
Active geo-replication with a secondary database in each of the three regions
Geo-restore of the latest backup into each region every night
why: Active geo-replication supports multiple readable secondaries, in different regions, and failover is always initiated by an administrator. A failover group replicates to a single secondary server, so it cannot place copies in three regions. Read scale-out only reads from replicas inside the primary's own region. Nightly geo-restores produce copies that are many hours stale and are not continuously replicated.

q: A third-party application on two Azure VMs depends on SQL Agent jobs, logins, and linked servers, which must fail over automatically with the databases without being re-created on a second server. Azure shared disks are available. Which technology fits?
opts: An Always On availability group with synchronous commit covering all user databases
A Failover Cluster Instance on a Windows Server Failover Cluster using shared disks
Log shipping to a warm standby instance on the second VM
Backup to URL with scripted restores onto the second VM
why: A Failover Cluster Instance fails over the whole instance, so msdb jobs, logins, and linked servers move with it. An availability group replicates only the chosen user databases, leaving jobs and logins to be created and kept in sync on each replica. Log shipping also moves databases only and fails over manually. Scripted restores from backup are slower and entirely manual.

q: Compliance requires each year's first full backup to be retained for seven years, while operations wants to restore to any point within the last 14 days. Which configuration meets both?
opts: PITR retention of 14 days, plus an LTR policy retaining a yearly backup for seven years
PITR retention raised to seven years, with LTR left unconfigured
An LTR policy alone, because LTR backups also allow restore to any moment
PITR retention of 35 days, plus an LTR policy that keeps monthly backups for 30 days
why: PITR covers the short window with log-based restore to any moment, and an LTR policy with a yearly backup retained for seven years covers compliance, since the two retain backups independently. PITR retention tops out at 35 days, so seven years is impossible. LTR backups restore only to the moment each backup was taken, not to arbitrary points. A monthly policy kept for 30 days leaves nothing at year seven.

q: An active geo-replication secondary can be created on a different logical server in the same region as the primary.
opts: True
False
why: Geo-replication does not require a different region; a secondary on another server in the same region is allowed, for example to offload reads or to move a database. It is the failover-group and disaster-recovery designs that usually place the secondary in another region.

q: A Failover Cluster Instance keeps a synchronized copy of the data on each node, so losing the shared storage does not cause an outage.
opts: True
False
why: An FCI has one copy of the data on shared storage and nothing is synchronized between nodes, so a storage failure is outside what it covers and is addressed beneath it with storage-level resilience such as Storage Spaces Direct or replication. An availability group is the design that keeps separate synchronized copies on each replica.

q: A long-term retention backup can be restored to any point in time within its retention period, just as a PITR restore can.
opts: True
False
why: An LTR backup is a copy of a specific full backup, so a restore returns the database to the moment that backup was taken, not to arbitrary points. Restoring to an arbitrary moment depends on log backups kept only for the shorter PITR window.

q: Which two statements about auto-failover groups are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The read-only listener endpoint always points at the current secondary, so it follows role changes
A forced failover can lose transactions that had not yet replicated to the secondary
After a failover, clients must switch to the secondary server's own name
Automatic failover triggers immediately on any transient error in a single database
why: The read-only listener tracks whichever server is currently secondary, and replication is asynchronous, so forcing a failover can drop transactions that had not yet arrived. Clients keep using the listener names after failover, and automatic failover is governed by a grace period precisely so that transient errors do not trigger it.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish an FCI from a traditional availability group? (Choose two.)
opts: Logins and SQL Agent jobs are not replicated by an availability group, so each replica needs them
An FCI keeps one copy of the data on shared storage, so storage failure is not covered
An FCI can offload reporting queries to a readable passive node
An availability group requires all of its replicas to attach to the same shared volume
why: An availability group replicates user databases only, so server-level objects such as logins and jobs must be kept in sync by hand, while an FCI has one copy of the data on shared storage that it does not protect itself. A passive FCI node is not readable, and availability group replicas keep separate storage rather than sharing a volume.

q: Which two statements about point-in-time restore in Azure SQL Database are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A deleted database can still be restored to a point before deletion within the retention period
A restore produces a new database, so the original keeps running until the DBA swaps names
A restore can only target the moments when full backups were taken
PITR retention can be raised to 90 days without configuring long-term retention
why: Backups of a deleted database are retained for its retention period, so it can be restored, and a PITR restore always creates a new database instead of overwriting the original. Transaction log backups let PITR target arbitrary moments, not only full-backup times. PITR retention is capped at 35 days, so longer retention needs LTR.

q: A Business Critical database must stay available if one availability zone in its region is lost. There will be no second region and no failover group. Which change meets this?
opts: Zone-redundant backup storage
Zone-redundant configuration for the database
Active geo-replication to a secondary in the same region
Read scale-out enabled on the database
why: Zone-redundant configuration places the database's replicas in different availability zones, so a zone loss triggers failover inside the region. Zone-redundant backup storage protects only the backup copies, not the running database. A same-region geo-secondary is not guaranteed to sit in another zone and has to be failed over manually. Read scale-out only routes read traffic to an existing replica.

q: When a zone-redundant database fails over because an availability zone is lost, the application's connection string does not need to change.
opts: True
False
why: Zone redundancy fails over between replicas inside the same logical server and region, so the server name and database name stay the same and applications only need ordinary retry logic. Only cross-region designs involve a second server, and even then a failover group's listener hides it.

q: Which two statements about zone-redundant Azure SQL Database are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Failover between zones is automatic and keeps the same server and database names
It does not cover a regional outage; a failover group or geo-replication adds that
It provides readable secondaries in other regions for reporting
A zone-redundant database cannot be added to an auto-failover group
why: Zone redundancy fails over automatically between zones within the same region, so names do not change, and it does nothing for a full-region loss, which is the job of cross-region features. It adds no cross-region replicas, and a zone-redundant database can participate in a failover group, so the two protections are layered.

q: After an automatic failover of a failover group, an application using the group's listener name keeps working, while a second application that used the original primary server's name fails. Why?
opts: The second application targets the old primary, now the secondary; the listener repoints
Listener endpoints support only read-only connections after a failover has completed
The first application uses connection pooling, which masked the outage from its users
A failover renames the new primary to the old primary's server name
why: The failover group's read-write listener always resolves to whichever server is currently primary, while a hard-coded server name keeps pointing at a server that now holds the secondary role. The listener serves read-write connections after failover. Pooling does not hide a change of primary. Failovers swap roles and do not rename servers.

q: Reporting must run against the secondary of a failover group without hard-coding a server name, and must keep targeting the secondary after roles swap. What should the reporting tool use?
opts: The failover group's read-only listener endpoint
The secondary server's own name, updated by hand after any failover
The read-write listener endpoint with ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly
The original primary's name with read scale-out enabled
why: The read-only listener endpoint always resolves to the current secondary, so reporting follows role changes with no connection-string edits. A hard-coded secondary name breaks after a swap and needs manual updates. The read-write listener resolves to the primary, and intent alone does not move the session to the geo-secondary. Read scale-out uses an HA replica in the primary's own region, not the geo-secondary.

q: A region hosting an Azure SQL Database is unavailable. The database had no failover group or geo-replication, and its backups use geo-redundant storage. What recovery is possible, and what is the consequence?
opts: Geo-restore in another region, losing data after the last replicated backup
Instant promotion of the hidden secondary every database keeps in the paired region
A point-in-time restore on the original server to the moment just before the outage
Zone-redundant failover to a different region, with no data loss
why: Geo-restore rebuilds the database in another region from geo-redundant backups, so recovery is slower and loses whatever was not yet in the replicated backups, with restore time growing with size. Databases keep no hidden cross-region secondary. A point-in-time restore uses backups in the unavailable region. Zone redundancy never leaves the region.

q: A production database must remain recoverable in another region if its home region is lost, but the team wants no standing secondary and the lowest cost that allows this. Which backup storage redundancy should be selected?
opts: Locally redundant backup storage
Zone-redundant backup storage
Geo-redundant backup storage
Locally redundant storage plus a database-level firewall rule
why: Geo-redundant backup storage copies backups to the paired region, which is what geo-restore needs after a regional loss, with no standing replica to pay for. Locally redundant storage keeps copies in a single datacenter, and zone-redundant storage spreads them across zones inside the one region, so neither survives a regional loss. A firewall rule has no effect on where backups are stored.

q: Which two statements about instance failover groups on Managed Instance are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Every user database on the instance is replicated, with no way to exclude individual ones
The two instances need network connectivity between their virtual networks, such as peering or a gateway
Individual databases can be added to or removed from the group at any time
There are no listener endpoints, so apps must use the secondary instance's own name after failover
why: An instance failover group works at whole-instance scope, replicating all user databases, and the two instances must be able to communicate across their virtual networks. Per-database membership is a feature of single-database failover groups and geo-replication. Instance failover groups do provide read-write and read-only listener endpoints so connection strings stay stable.

q: A company must migrate an on-premises SQL Server 2022 database to Managed Instance with minimal downtime, keep both synchronized until cutover, and retain the option to fail back to the on-premises server if a problem appears afterward. Which approach fits?
opts: The Managed Instance link
Azure Database Migration Service in online mode using log replay
Native backup and restore from Blob Storage
Transactional replication from the on-premises publisher to the instance
why: The Managed Instance link keeps the databases continuously synchronized and supports a planned failover that can also be reversed, which gives the fail-back path. DMS online migration using log replay also minimizes downtime, but it is a one-way migration with no supported return. Native backup and restore is an offline copy. Transactional replication can reduce downtime but is not a rollback-capable cutover mechanism.

q: A team runs SQL Server on an Azure VM and wants policy-based full, differential, and log backups with central management, without writing or maintaining backup scripts. Which option fits?
opts: Azure Backup for SQL Server, with a policy in a Recovery Services vault
Long-term retention policies configured on the databases of the VM
A SQL Agent job per database that runs BACKUP DATABASE ... TO URL
Geo-restore configured against the VM's disks and data files
why: Azure Backup for SQL Server in Azure VMs provides workload-aware full, differential, and log backups through a vault policy, with central monitoring and no scripts. Long-term retention is a PaaS feature that does not apply to a VM. A job per database calling BACKUP ... TO URL works but is exactly the scripting the team wants to avoid. Geo-restore recovers PaaS databases from service-managed backups and does not apply to VM disks.

q: Which two statements about read-only routing on an Always On availability group listener are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The client must connect through the listener and set ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly
Each target secondary must allow read-only connections and have a read-only routing URL
It works with a Basic availability group, whose secondary accepts read-only connections
It works with an FCI, because the passive node accepts read-only connections
why: Routing happens at the listener and depends on the connection declaring read intent, and each target secondary must be readable and have a routing URL configured. A Basic availability group's secondary cannot accept connections, and an FCI's passive node is not readable, so routing has nowhere to send traffic in those designs.

q: A standards body requires an annual disaster recovery test for a Managed Instance protected by a failover group. The test must run in production, must not risk data loss, and must prove the application works afterward. What should the DBA do?
opts: Rename the production database to break connectivity, then geo-restore it onto another instance
Delete the secondary instance and recreate it from backups
Perform a forced failover with data loss allowed, to simulate a real regional outage
Perform a planned failover to the secondary, validate the application, and fail back
why: A planned failover synchronizes the pair before swapping roles, so it loses no data and can be used as a production drill, and failing back is a second planned failover. Forced failover can lose data, the rename-and-geo-restore drill is the approach for databases without a failover group and is best done on a test copy, and deleting the secondary tests nothing and removes protection.

q: The secondary instance in a Managed Instance failover group exists only for disaster recovery and serves no read workload. How can the company avoid paying SQL Server licensing for the secondary's vCores?
opts: Switch the secondary to the DTU purchasing model
Enable read scale-out so that the secondary earns a discount
Designate the secondary as a standby replica to use the failover rights benefit
Stop the failover group and rely on geo-restore
why: Designating the secondary as standby grants the failover rights benefit for the vCores licensed on the primary, while compute and storage are still billed. Managed Instance has no DTU model, removing the failover group removes the low-RPO protection the company wants, and serving read workloads would make the replica ineligible for the standby designation.

q: An Azure SQL Database is geo-replicated. Which view, queried on the primary, shows how many seconds the geo-secondary is behind?
opts: sys.resource_stats in the master database, in the storage_in_megabytes column
sys.dm_db_resource_stats, in the avg_log_write_percent column
sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, in the log_send_queue_size column
sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status, in the replication_lag_sec column
why: sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status reports replication state, the last replication time, and replication_lag_sec for an Azure SQL Database geo-replication link. sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states is for availability groups on SQL Server and linked replicas, and the resource views report utilization and storage, not replication lag.
